surya-namaskara-intro.title: Surya Namaskara
notes: The practice of the Surya Namaskara has come down from the long distant past, and is capable of rendering human life heavenly and blissful.
Following the ancestors' traditions and practices develops the body and mind and makes possible the realization of the nature of the Self.

By the precept 'Shariramadyam khalu dharma Sadhanam' — the first duty is to take care of the body, the means to the pursuit of spiritual life — the ancestors found the means to bodily health through the Surya Namaskara and the limbs of yoga.
The shastras explain the meaning of mantras so that even dull minds can understand them; among them are those that elucidate mantras addressed to the Sun God.
The Surya Namaskara should always be practiced in the Namaskara form, in accordance with the method prescribed in the shastra, not whimsically.

The tradition of the Surya Namaskara follows the method of vinyasa (breathing and movement), rechaka (exhalation), puraka (inhalation), and meditation; sun salutations done without following these rules are little more than exercise, not true Surya Namaskara.
There are two types of Surya Namaskara: the first has nine vinyasas, the second seventeen.
To learn the vinyasas, rechaka and puraka, the bandhas, dhyana, and trataka, one should consult a Satguru; it would be wrong to try to learn yoga without recourse to such a teacher.
Kumbhaka, or breath retention, does not occur either in the Surya Namaskara or in the asanas, and this method is best learned from a Guru.
For those who practice asanas, the Surya Namaskara must be performed first, followed by the asanas; after finishing, worship should be performed sitting in Padmasana.
quotes: Shariramadyam khalu dharma Sadhanam [The first duty is to take care of the body, which is the means to the pursuit of spiritual life].
Thus, if the scriptural way of practicing the Surya Namaskara is followed, the most terrible diseases, such as leprosy, epilepsy, and jaundice, will be cured.
Aspirants should know this method, which is best learned from a Guru.

swadhyaya.title: Swadhyaya
swadhyaya.one_line: The recital of Vedic verses and prayers in accordance with strict rules of recitation.
points: Swadhyaya is the recital of Vedic verses and prayers in accordance with strict rules of recitation.

Vedic hymns must be recited without damaging the artha (meaning) and Devata (deity) of a mantra through a wrong swara (pitch) or improper articulation of akshara (letter), pada (word), or varna (sentence).

The Gayatri mantra forms the basis for the study of all Vedic verses; mantras fall into Vedic (pragita and apragita) and Tantric (strilinga, pullinga, and napumsakalinga) categories, whose nature must be learned from a text called the Mantra Rahasya.
Guruji notes that such mantras are not very helpful to raja yoga and puts off discussing them.
Gods related to the mantras give siddhis (powers) to those who chant them and ponder their meanings, and a Satguru should be consulted to learn their secrets.

sutra.translation: Owing to the learning and application of personal mantras, there is union with (one's) desired deity.

tapas.title: Tapas
tapas.one_line: Observances performed to discipline the body and sense organs.
points: Tapas means observances performed to discipline the body and sense organs.

Guruji quotes the Yoga Yagnavalkya: sages well-versed in austerity say that performing penances such as krchra and chandrayana (food regulation in accordance with the lunar cycles), which discipline the body in accordance with the scriptures, is the greatest of all tapas.
Tapas that follow the injunctions of the shastras should be regarded as great.
By means of tapas, impurities are destroyed, the antah karana (the inner instrument of mind, intellect, ego, and discrimination) becomes purified, and the body and sense organs are perfected.

sutra.translation: The perfection of the body and sense organs is due to intensity in spiritual practice, being the elimination of impurities.

tiriangmukhaikapada-paschimattanasana.title: Tiriangmukhaikapada Paschimattanasana
notes: The methods of vinyasa are the same as those for Ardha Baddha Padma Paschimattanasana.
The method of inhaling and exhaling for each vinyasa follows the same pattern throughout the asanas.

Through the 6th vinyasa of the first Surya Namaskara, the opening vinyasas are the same for all the asanas. All asanas conclude with uth pluthi (lifting up off the floor with the strength of the arms), then a jump back into the 4th vinyasa of the Surya Namaskara, followed by the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th vinyasas.

sequence.action: Vinyasas 1–6 as in the first Surya Namaskara.

At the 7th vinyasa, jump through the arms, sit as described in Paschimattanasana, stretch the left leg out, fold the right leg back, placing the right foot by the side of the thigh, join the knees together, take hold with both hands of the left foot, which is at a right angle to the floor, lift the head and chest up fully.
Slowly place the forehead on the outstretched leg, and do puraka and rechaka as much as possible.
Slowly lift the head only.
Do the 11th vinyasa described in Paschimattanasana.
Vinyasas 11–13 follow the 4th, 5th, and 6th vinyasas of the first Surya Namaskara.

Again sitting in the 7th vinyasa of Paschimattanasana, stretch out the right leg, fold back the left leg in the same manner as the right leg above, take hold of the right foot with both hands, and lift the head and chest up.
Slowly place the forehead on the outstretched knee, and do puraka and rechaka as much as possible.
Slowly lift up only the head.
The 17th vinyasa follows the method of the 10th vinyasa. The 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd vinyasas follow the 4th, 5th, 6th, 3rd, and 2nd vinyasas of Paschimattanasana.

while_holding: Rechaka and puraka slowly and as much as possible.
benefits: Tiriangmukhaikapada Paschimattanasana cures a number of afflictions, including: body fat; water retention; thighs swollen out of proportion to the size of the body (elephant leg); piles; and sciatica.
It also makes the body symmetrical.
cautions: Readers and aspirants should learn these fully, which is best done under the guidance of a Guru.

ubhaya-padangushtasana.title: Ubhaya Padangushtasana

sequence.action: Having reached the 7th vinyasa of Supta Padangushtasana, lie down and join the legs.
Straighten both legs, as in Sarvangasana.
As in Halasana, bring the legs up over the head, place the feet on the floor, and tightly take hold of the big toes.
Without letting go of the toes, roll forward and come to sit purely on the buttocks in the manner of Navasana, doing rechaka and puraka.
Remaining vinyasas as in earlier asanas.

while_holding: Both rechaka and puraka occur in the 8th vinyasa.
In the 9th vinyasa, do rechaka and puraka slowly and as much as possible, keeping the chest lifted and the stomach drawn in fully.
benefits: Ubhaya Padangushtasana is an asana that purifies the anus, waist, stomach, genital organs, and the granthi traya, or the three knots below the vina danda, which begin at the anal canal.
It also eliminates the burning sensation that can occur during urination.

upavishta-konasana.title: Upavishta Konasana

sequence.action: Vinyasas 1–6 as in the first Surya Namaskara.

Without touching the floor, jump the legs through the arms on the strength of the arms, spread the legs as wide as possible, sit with straightened knees, take hold of the sides of the feet, and lift the head and chest.
Pull in the stomach, slowly place the head and chest on the floor, and do puraka and rechaka slowly, as much as possible.
Lift only the head.
Without losing hold of the sides of the feet, prepare to come up.
Come up to sit straight on the buttocks, still holding the feet.
Hold the raised legs wide apart and straight, as in the 8th vinyasa, keep the chest, arms, and waist straight, look up, and do rechaka and puraka as much as possible.
Remaining vinyasas as in earlier asanas.

while_holding: Holding mula bandha and uddiyana bandha is very important.
As practice becomes firm, rest the chin on the floor in the state of this asana while holding the feet.
benefits: If the nadi called grdhrasi [sciatic nerve], which is in the mid-region between the anus and the organ of generation, becomes weak, then the strength of the waist will decrease, and the other nadis will weaken as well. When the grdhrasi nadi is weak, the waist becomes stiff and sitting and walking become difficult. Through the practice of this asana, however, such afflictions will go.

With the return of the grdhrasi nadi’s strength, other nadis and organs also will become strong, and udara bhramana [gaseous movements in the stomach] will no longer occur, and peristalsis will be resolved.
cautions: The practice of Upavishta Konasana, however, is not appropriate for pregnant women.

urdhva-mukha-paschimattanasana.title: Urdhva Mukha Paschimattanasana

sequence.action: Lie in the 8th vinyasa of Ubhaya Padangushtasana, and take hold of the sides of the feet near the heels.
Come into the state of Ubhaya Padangushtasana with straightened knees, sitting firmly on the buttocks while holding the feet, not the toes.
Place the face between the knees slowly, then do puraka and rechaka.
Slowly come back into the 9th vinyasa of Ubhaya Padangushtasana, and sit.
Remaining vinyasas as in Paschimattanasana.

benefits: Urdhva Mukha Paschimattanasana purifies the katti granthi [lower back], the esophagus, and the swadishtana chakra, or region between the anus and navel.
When the swadishtana chakra is purified, bodily activities become light, all physical activities are free and easy, and impediments, such as disease, do not torture one.

urdhva-padmasana.title: Urdhva Padmasana

sequence.action: Do all vinyasas through to the state of Sarvangasana.
Maintaining the same state, do Padmasana.
Unlock the legs and come into the 4th vinyasa of Sarvangasana.
Remaining vinyasas as in Sarvangasana.

while_holding: Tighten the anus, draw in the stomach fully, hold the knees with the hands, straighten the arms, and slowly do puraka and rechaka as much as possible.
benefits: Urdhva Padmasana purifies the anal and urinary channels, and causes the anterior section of the spinal column to become firm.

By means of these five asanas, the vishuddhi chakra [throat chakra], heart, lungs, limbs, digestive system, and jathara [stomach] are purified, and perversions of the vital wind, which result in hiccups, dry cough, constipation, and indigestion, as well as high blood pressure, are warded off.
They also prevent illnesses such as asthma, and ailments related to the heart.
urdhva-padmasana.benefits_source: Given in the book under Pindasana, as the benefits of asanas 32 to 36; the last two apply to all five.

uth-pluthi.title: Uth Pluthi
notes: While not an actual asana, Uth Pluthi is nevertheless highly beneficial.

Sarvangasana, Halasana, Karnapidasana, Urdhva Padmasana, Pindasana, Matsyasana, Uttana Padasana, Shirshasana, and Padmasana should only be practiced after the other asanas have been completed; after these nine, no further asanas should be done. Those who do only a limited number of asanas daily should include these nine.

sequence.action: At the conclusion of Padmasana and without releasing the legs, press the hands firmly on the floor on either side of the thighs and, on the force of the hands alone, lift the body up off the floor. Stay, doing rechaka and puraka fully as much as possible.
Jump back into the 4th vinyasa of the first Surya Namaskara and follow the vinyasas described in earlier asanas.
Jump through the arms, lie down, and rest for five minutes. This concludes the practice.

while_holding: Keep the arms, spine, and neck completely straight, the chin tilted down a little.
benefits: Uth Pluthi is useful for strengthening the waist and perfecting abdominal and anal control.
The three granthis, located in the sacrum, gradually open completely.
quotes: If aspirants heed this advice and carefully practice the asanas described above, then they will have the means to prosperity, both material and spiritual.

utkatasana.title: Utkatasana
notes: The vinyasa method described for the first Surya Namaskara is important to know for this asana.
Rechaka and puraka for the first six vinyasas must be performed in the same manner as in the first Surya Namaskara.
The vinyasas of the asanas that follow begin as they do for the first six vinyasas of the first Surya Namaskara; from the 7th vinyasa on, the vinyasas, and rechaka and puraka, differ for each asana.

sequence.action: Vinyasas 1–6 as in the first Surya Namaskara.
After the 6th vinyasa, jump into the 1st vinyasa of the second Surya Namaskara, and perform rechaka and puraka as much as possible.
Press the hands to the floor by the sides of the feet, put the whole weight of the body on the two hands, and lift the body up off the floor.
Throw the body back with the force of the arms, and hold the position, as in the 4th vinyasa of the first Surya Namaskara.
Do the 5th vinyasa of the Surya Namaskara.
Do the 6th vinyasa of the Surya Namaskara.
Do the 3rd vinyasa of the Surya Namaskara.
Do the 2nd vinyasa of the Surya Namaskara.
Return to Samasthiti.

benefits: Utkatasana increases the strength of the waist, which becomes slender, and makes the body light.
It also prevents pain associated with the vertebral column.
cautions: Again, no asana should be performed without following the proper method of vinyasa.
I consider it my earnest duty to caution the reader and aspirant not to try to learn these methods from books, reflections [photos], or pseudo-yogis.

uttana-padasana.title: Uttana Padasana
notes: In consolidated practice: after Sarvangasana, do Halasana, then the state of Karnapidasana, then Urdhva Padmasana, then Pindasana; finishing puraka, move into the state of Matsyasana while doing rechaka; then pass into the state of Uttana Padasana; and finally, doing puraka and rechaka, do Chakrasana.

sequence.action: Perform all the vinyasas from the beginning of Sarvangasana to the 7th vinyasa.

As in Matsyasana, lift the head, place the crown of the head on the floor, arch the back, extend the legs as in Navasana, hold straightened arms out parallel with the legs, bring the palms together, and tighten the entire body. Stay, doing rechaka and puraka as much as possible.
Do the 9th vinyasa of Matsyasana, and roll into the 4th vinyasa of the first Surya Namaskara.
The next vinyasas follow those of earlier asanas.

benefits: Matsyasana and Uttana Padasana counterpose the five asanas that precede them and remove the shoulder and waist pain that result from their practice.
They also purify the esophagus and anus, as well as the liver and spleen, and furnish the waist and neck with increasing strength.
uttana-padasana.benefits_source: Given in the book for Matsyasana and Uttana Padasana together.

utthita-hasta-padangushtasana.title: Utthita Hasta Padangushtasana

sequence.action: Join the legs together, hold the arms by the sides, and stand erect.
Place the left hand on the waist, straighten the right arm, raise the right leg, catch hold of the big toe with the right hand, and straighten the knees, chest, and waist.
Holding this posture, touch the nose to the knee, which is lifted, and hold, doing puraka and rechaka as much as possible.
Slowly lift the head, straighten the chest and waist, and stand as in the 1st vinyasa.
Bring the right leg out to the right, hold the arm, leg, waist, and chest straight, and look to the left, breathing fully and deeply as much as possible.
Bring the leg back to the center, as in the 1st vinyasa.
Keeping the leg lifted, touch the nose to the right knee.

Lift the head, straighten the chest and waist, and stand straight, placing the hands on the waist and keeping the raised right leg extended straight, while breathing fully and deeply as much as possible.
Bring the right leg down.
Repeat the above for the left leg.

benefits: Utthita Hasta Padangushtasana loosens the hip joints, destroys defects of the testicles and male organ of generation, and purifies and strengthens the vertebral column, waist, hips, and lower abdomen.
It also eliminates constipation.

utthita-parshvakonasana.title: Utthita Parshvakonasana

sequence.action: Jump the legs open to the right and stand with the legs as much as five feet apart, as in Trikonasana, stretching out the arms tightly at the level of the chest, and swelling the chest.

Turn the right foot out, bend the knee completely, place the right hand by the side of the right foot, stretch the left arm straight out over the ear, and gaze at the fingertips. Puraka and rechaka should be done as much as possible.
Return to the position of the 1st vinyasa.
Repeat, as with the right leg, for the left leg.
Return to the position of the 1st vinyasa.
Return to Samasthiti.

while_holding: Hold the body tightly.
Rechaka and puraka slowly and as much as possible.
benefits: Utthita Parshvakonasana purifies the ribs and lower abdomen, dissolves the bad fat at the waist, and softens the limbs so that subsequent asanas can be more easily practiced.

utthita-trikonasana.title: Utthita Trikonasana
notes: Rechaka and puraka should be performed as above; as with the Surya Namaskara, rechaka occurs on the even-numbered vinyasas and puraka on the odd.

sequence.action: Jump the legs open to the right, three feet apart, stretch the arms out wide on either side of the torso at chest level, and hold.

Turn the right foot to the right, reach down and take hold of the big toe of the right foot with the right hand, lift up the other arm, fix the gaze on its fingertips, and do puraka and rechaka slowly and as much as possible. Both knees must be kept straight.
Return to the position of the 1st vinyasa, and hold.
Turn the left foot to the left, reach down and take hold of the big toe, gaze at the tip of the raised hand, and do puraka and rechaka as much as possible.
Return to the position of the 1st vinyasa.
Return to Samasthiti.

benefits: Utthita Trikonasana dissolves the bad fat at the waist, and brings the body into shape.
It also expands the narrow portion of the breathing channel and strengthens the backbone.

virabhadrasana.title: Virabhadrasana
notes: When in the states of Utkatasana and Virabhadrasana, there is no need to do rechaka and puraka more than five times.
Aspirants should not forget to do rechaka and puraka while performing the vinyasas.
While in the asana's state, it is always important that the body be held firmly and steadily.

sequence.action: Vinyasas 1–6 as in the first Surya Namaskara.
Stand as in the 7th vinyasa of the second Surya Namaskara, and do rechaka and puraka five times.
Turn to the left, bend the left knee, keeping the arms raised over the head, with the palms together, the chest lifted up, and do puraka and rechaka five times.
Keeping the legs in the same position, bring arms down to shoulder level, and stand gazing at the fingertips of the left hand, keeping the arms stretched out straight and tight.
Without bending the arms, turn to the right, bend the right knee, and stand gazing at the tips of the right hand with concentration.

Place the hands on the floor on either side of the right foot and, without allowing the legs to touch the floor, lift both the left leg and bent right leg completely off the floor with only the strength of the hands.
Vinyasas 12–16 as the 4th, 5th, 6th, 3rd, and 2nd vinyasas of the first Surya Namaskara, respectively.

benefits: By means of Virabhadrasana, all the joints of the body, as well as the lower abdomen, spinal column, and organ of generation, are purified.
In addition, pain associated with the knees, as well as the pain from standing or sitting all day while working, is eliminated.
cautions: Again, it is best to learn the vinyasas of all the asanas, as well as their states and the series of rechaka and puraka, under the guidance of a Guru, as these are very difficult to relate in the written descriptions given here.

what-is-yoga.title: What Is Yoga?
what-is-yoga.one_line: Yoga is the means by which the mind is established in the Self, not merely a physical practice or a word to be understood intellectually.
points: The practice of yoga is not new to India; it is a noble, desireless action, coupled with righteousness, passed down in an unbroken tradition since time immemorial.
Guruji writes that people today experience pleasure, disease, or yoga in accordance with their karma, and that from pleasure, disease is certain.
The word yoga has many meanings — relation, means, union, knowledge, matter, logic — but its core sense here is upaya, the path or way by which something is attained.
Just as a servant seeks a king, a disciple seeks a Guru, and a wife seeks her husband, so the mind should seek the Universal Self; establishing the mind in the Self is yoga.
Patanjali's aphorism is quoted: "Yoga chitta vritti nirodhaha" — yoga is the process of ending the definitions of the field of consciousness.
The sense organs grasp objects only through the mind; yoga is the means by which the mind is directed toward the Self and prevented from going toward outside objects, as the Katha Upanishad states.
Mere intellectual study of yoga's meaning does not realize its benefits, just as knowledge of culinary science does not satisfy hunger — the scriptures show the path, but practice is required.

By the grace of the Guru and constant practice, an aspirant can realize the Indweller — the nature of supreme peace and eternal bliss, and the cause of creation, sustenance, and destruction of the universe — before death.
Ashtanga yoga, the eight-limbed path, is what teaches how to make the mind one-pointed so as to see the Universal Self.

sutra.sanskrit: Sri Gurum Gananatham cha Vanim shanmathuram tatha Yogeshwaram Sri Harim cha Pranat'osmi moohoormuhu.
sutra.translation: To the blessed Guru and Ganesh, as well as to Saraswati and Skanda, to Shiva, the lord of the yogis, and Shri Hari, I bow again and again.

verses.sanskrit: Vande Gurunam charanaravinde / Sandarshita svatmasukhavabodhe / Nishreyase jangalikayamane / Samsara halahala mohashantyai.
verses.translation: I worship the Guru’s lotus feet / Awakening the happiness of the Self revealed / Beyond comparison, acting like the jungle physician / To pacify delusion from the poison of existence.

yama.title: Yama
yama.one_line: The first limb of ashtanga yoga, consisting of five ethical restraints.
points: Yama is the first of the eight limbs of ashtanga yoga.
It consists of five parts: ahimsa; satya; asteya; brahmacharya; and aparigraha.

Guruji writes that each of the five sub-limbs is associated with yama, the first limb, and that only the actions of previous lives will lead us to practice them; the mind turns to the practice of yoga only when a samskara or vasana is present.
Even where a samskara exists, aspirants must expect to practice the yogic steps with effort.

guruji.name: Sri K. Pattabhi Jois
life: Born on the full moon day of July in the small village of Kowshika, in the Hassan district of Karnataka State, South India.

His father was an astrologer, priest, and landholder; from the age of five he was instructed in Sanskrit and rituals by his father, as were all Brahmin boys. His mother cared for the house and their nine children, of whom Jois was the fifth.

In October–November 1927, at age twelve, he attended a lecture-demonstration by Sri T. Krishnamacharya in Hassan, was amazed by the asanas, and the next day asked to be instructed in yoga, beginning a twenty-five-year period of study with him.
For two years he practiced with Krishnamacharya daily in Kowshika without telling his family he was learning yoga.

In 1930, without informing anyone, he left Kowshika for Mysore with two rupees in his pocket to attend the maharaja's Sanskrit College, begging for food and sleeping in a friend's dormitory room; it was three years before he wrote to tell his father where he was.
He remained at the Sanskrit College from 1930 to 1956, studying Sanskrit and then the Vedas, and eventually earned a professorship in Advaita Vedanta; he taught there until 1973.

In 1931 he was reunited with Krishnamacharya at a demonstration at the Sanskrit College. A minister from the palace of the Maharaja of Mysore, Krishna Rajendra Wodeyar, was also present; the maharaja became Krishnamacharya's patron and established a yoga shala for him on the palace grounds.
On March 1, 1937, at the maharaja's invitation, Jois began to teach at the Sanskrit College.
In 1948, in his home in Lakshmipurum, he established the Ashtanga Yoga Research Institute; in 1964 he built an extension for the yoga hall and a resting room upstairs.
He began writing Yoga Mala by hand in 1958, working little by little over a two- to three-year period in the afternoons while his family rested; it was first published in India in 1962.

A Belgian named André van Lysebeth studied the primary and intermediate asanas with him and later published a photograph of Guruji and his address, through which his whereabouts became known in Europe.
In 1973 the first Americans came to study with him, after his son Manju demonstrated yoga at Swami Gitananda's ashram in Pondicherry.

In 1974 he made his first trip to the West, by invitation of Marie Helena Bastidos to a yoga conference in South America, where he lectured on yoga in Sanskrit; in 1975 he traveled to California with Manju.
He taught tirelessly at his yoga institute for seventy years.
guruji.life_source: From the forewords by Eddie Stern and R. Sharath.

summary: Guruji writes of his great pleasure that yogic practice, part of Indian culture, has gained recognition and respect not only in India but in Western countries as well.
He notes that scriptures, puranas, Vedas, and legends show the science of yoga has existed in India since time immemorial, but that as years passed and times changed, it reached a very low state.

He describes differences of opinion about yoga: that its practice is only a form of physical exercise; that it is useful only to sannyasins living an absolute celibate life, so family men should abstain from it; and that some people fear practicing it at all.

He compares these doubts to judging sugar by its faults without knowing its sweetness, saying that once we taste it, its sweetness becomes apparent, and once we practice yoga, we come to realize its ananda (bliss).

He observes that the practice of yoga still leaves us subject to doubts and misconceptions that weaken our minds and sense organs, so that we experience suffering without seeing material or spiritual prosperity.
He invokes the Bhagavad Gita's teaching that the sacred teaching (shastra) is our measure in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done.
He states that if we practice the science of yoga without fail, we will attain physical, mental, and spiritual happiness, and it was with this great desire that he wrote the book.
quotes: “Tasmat shastram pramanam te karya akarya vyavasthitau [Therefore, the sacred teaching (shastra) is your measure in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done].”
Once they taste it, its sweetness becomes apparent.
It is with this great desire that I have written this book.

blessing.summary: The blessing from Sri Shringeri Jagadguru Mahasamsthanam (Sharada Pitham) is a benediction given by His Holiness of Sri Shringeri Mutt for Yoga Mala. It states that Guruji, after a deep study of the philosophy and practice of yoga and personal enjoyment of its fruits, was endeavoring to spread its knowledge and benefits, and that the text of Yoga Mala is the fruit of his labor. It corrects the impression that yoga is fit only for those free from passions and attachment, noting that many of its postures, breathing techniques, and restraints contribute to physical and mental health generally, and that some illnesses considered incurable by modern medicine may be curable by yogic postures and breath control. It closes with the hope that the book would be published and prove beneficial to a great many people.
quotes: The text of Yoga Mala is the fruit of his labor.
Various postures, breathing techniques, and other restraints and self controls contribute not only to physical health, but to mental health as well.
Which posture is suited to which illness is very well described in Yoga Mala.
